title.en: A Mind for Concepts, Not Facts
title.de: Ein Kopf für Konzepte, nicht für Fakten

excerpt.en: I don't retain specifics well — dates, names, exact figures slip away. But give me the shape of how things relate and I never lose it. On thinking in relationships.
excerpt.de: Ich behalte Details schlecht — Daten, Namen, genaue Zahlen entgleiten mir. Aber gib mir die Form, wie Dinge zusammenhängen, und ich verliere sie nie. Über das Denken in Beziehungen.

body.en:
My memory for specifics is bad in a way that used to embarrass me. Dates, names, exact figures — they don't stick. What *does* stick, permanently, is the shape of how things relate: the structure, the cause-and-effect, the pattern.

For a long time I treated that as a deficiency. Now I think it's just a different storage format — lossy on facts, high-fidelity on relationships.

## How it actually works

- I can't recall the number, but I know exactly *why* it matters and what it connects to.
- I forget the exact syntax but remember the model it implements.
- I lose the quote but keep the idea it was pointing at.

## The upside and the tax

- Upside: concepts transfer across domains; facts don't. This is the engine of systems thinking.
- Tax: I have to look things up constantly, and I have to *externalize* facts (notes, references) instead of trusting recall.

## Notes to self

- Reframe honestly — not "bad memory," but "conceptual memory." Avoid making it sound like a superpower.
- Link to the note-taking post: externalizing facts is the compensating system.
